1247.title: what the Rig Veda is
1247.hook: a friend's replies go cold, and nobody will say why. In one Rig Veda hymn, the poet Vasishtha asks Varuna straight out: what did I do?
1247.howItsDone: Hymns to Varuna are read in Hindu tradition as prayers for release from wrongdoing, and the theme of asking forgiveness for faults, known and unknown, appears in prayers and rites of atonement.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: many gods, and one verse saying what is one, the wise speak of in many ways.
screen: `ONE, CALLED BY MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: The messages used to come every day. Jokes, photos, long voice notes. Now a friend answers in one word, or not at all. Something happened, but what? You scroll back looking for the moment it changed. You ask a mutual friend, carefully. They shrug: seems like they're upset with you. So there's one honest move left, and it's the hardest: go to the friend and ask, what did I do? A Rig Veda poet makes exactly that move, and the one he asks is a god.
screen: `THE MESSAGES GO QUIET.` → `SEEMS LIKE THEY'RE UPSET.` → `WHAT DID I DO?`

segments.voice: The god is Varuna. In the hymns, Varuna keeps rita, the right order of things, and he sees what people do. The poet is Vasishtha, a seer tradition remembers as the voice of these hymns. Something has gone wrong between them. In paraphrase, Vasishtha says: I ask about this wrong, Varuna, wanting to understand. I go to the wise to ask, and the sages all tell me the same thing: Varuna is angry with you. So he turns to Varuna himself. What was my great offense, he asks, that you would strike the friend who sings your praise? Tell me, and I'll come to you quickly, bowing, free of it. He asks to be released from the wrongs of his fathers, and from the ones he did himself. Then a startling line. It wasn't my own will, Varuna. It was drink, anger, the dice, thoughtlessness. The older one leads the younger astray. Even sleep doesn't keep wrongdoing away. Some readers hear an excuse in that. Others hear a man naming his weak spots out loud: strong drink, a temper, gambling, not thinking. Either way, he doesn't hide them. He brings them to the one he has wronged, and asks to be set right.
screen: `VARUNA SEES WHAT PEOPLE DO.` · `THE SAGES SAY: HE'S ANGRY.` · `WHAT WAS MY OFFENSE?` · `DRINK, ANGER, DICE, CARELESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Let one strained relationship come to mind, at home, at work, anywhere, and instead of arguing your side, ask quietly: what part of this might be mine? If something comes, name it plainly, the way Vasishtha named drink and anger and dice, with no punishment, just honesty; if you pray, you can bring that honesty to God in your own words.
What the Rig Veda is. Not only hymns of praise, but a seer asking Varuna what he did wrong, and naming his own weak spots out loud.

1248.title: what the Rig Veda is
1248.hook: a night-shift nurse walks out into a sky going pink. The Rig Veda sings to that light by name: Ushas, the dawn
1248.howItsDone: In Hindu practice, dawn is often a time of prayer: bathing, chanting, and offering water to the rising sun, and the hymns to Ushas are part of the Rig Veda's recited text.

segments.voice: The hospital doors slide open and a nurse steps out after a long night shift. Her feet hurt. Her head is full of beeping. Then she looks up. The sky over the parking lot is going from gray to rose to gold, and for a second she forgets everything else. The birds have started. A bus hisses at the corner. Plenty of mornings like this go by unseen. The Rig Veda's poets turned to that light, gave it a name, and sang to it. Today, Ushas, the dawn.
screen: `OUT OF THE NIGHT SHIFT.` → `GRAY, ROSE, GOLD.` → `THE POETS SANG TO IT.`

segments.voice: In the Rig Veda, Ushas is a goddess, pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, driving away the dark. One hymn to her begins, in paraphrase: this light has come, the fairest of lights. Her bright sign is born. Then the poet notices time. The night has made room for the dawn, like a sister giving way to her sister. And then this line. Gone are the mortals who watched the earlier dawns. Now she is seen by us. And coming are those who will see her in mornings still ahead. Three groups of people under one light: those before us, us, and those after. Every sunrise, on this reading, joins them. The same hymn ends by waking everyone up. Rise, it says. The breath of life has come back to us. The dark has gone away. Light is coming near. She has opened a path for the sun to travel. The hymn holds two things together: one life is short, and the light it's lived under is shared. And the dawn isn't new each day. She is ancient and young at once, the hymn says, coming again and again.
screen: `USHAS: THE DAWN, A GODDESS.` · `THE FAIREST OF LIGHTS HAS COME.` · `THOSE BEFORE, US, THOSE AFTER.` · `RISE: THE BREATH HAS COME BACK.`

segments.voice: Turn toward a window if you can, or call a dawn you remember to mind, and feel the light on your face, real or remembered. Hold three people in that same light: someone before you who saw this sky and is gone, someone with you now, someone who will see it after you; if you pray, you can greet the morning in your own way.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns that sing to Ushas, the dawn, fairest of lights, seen by those before us, by us, and by those still to come.

1249.title: what the Rig Veda is
1249.hook: a man swears off the slot machines, then hears the jingle from the next room. The Rig Veda keeps a gambler's own confession
1249.tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1249.howItsDone: The gambler's hymn is part of the Rig Veda's recited text, and Hindu teachers sometimes point to Savitar's advice in it, to leave the dice and tend one's field, as Vedic counsel against ruinous habits.

segments.voice: He promised. No more, not this time. He walks past the casino floor toward the exit, proud of himself. Then, from behind a row of machines, comes the bright little jingle of someone winning. His feet slow. The promise was real, and so is the pull, and the pull is winning. Anyone who has tried to quit a habit, a phone, a drink, may know that moment. One Rig Veda hymn is spoken by a gambler, in his own voice, and it doesn't hold back.
screen: `HE PROMISED. HE MEANT IT.` → `THEN THE SOUND OF WINNING.` → `A GAMBLER'S HYMN.`

segments.voice: He starts with the dice themselves. They thrill me, he says, in paraphrase, like a deep drink of soma. Then he tells what they cost. My wife never quarreled with me, never got angry. She was kind to me and to my friends. And for the sake of one losing throw, I drove away a devoted wife. Now his mother-in-law hates him, his wife pushes him away, and his own family says: we don't know him, take him away. Other men court his wife while the dice take his wealth. Then the line the hymn turns on. When I decide I won't play, he says, I fall behind as my friends go off. But when the brown dice are thrown and their sound reaches me, off I go to the meeting place like a lover to a lover. His resolve doesn't fail from lack of knowing better. It fails at the sound. Meanwhile his wife is left grieving, and his mother mourns a son wandering who knows where. Then a voice cuts through. Don't play with dice. Farm your field. Be glad of what you have, and value it. There are your cattle, there is your wife. So says Savitar, the god who rouses, linked with the sun. The hymn ends not at the gaming table but with a field, some cattle, and a wife at home.
screen: `THE DICE THRILL HIM LIKE SOMA.` · `HE DROVE AWAY A DEVOTED WIFE.` · `RESOLVE FAILS AT THE SOUND.` · `DON'T PLAY. FARM YOUR FIELD.`

segments.voice: Think of one pull that gets past your good intentions, a phone, a snack, an old argument you keep picking up, and without scolding yourself, notice its trigger: a sound, a time of day, a feeling. Then picture your field, the plain good things in front of you, and rest there; if you pray, you can ask for strength in your own words.
What the Rig Veda is. Hymns of fire, dawn and the one called by many names, and also a gambler's confession, ending with Savitar's advice: farm your field.

1250.title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1250.hook: rewind the day, then the year, then everything, until there's nothing left to rewind. The hymn of creation starts there, and starts with questions
1250.carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1250.tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1250.howItsDone: The Nasadiya Sukta is chanted as part of the Rig Veda's recited text and is also studied and discussed by Hindu teachers as a reflection on what came before creation.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, what the Rig Veda is: a gambler's confession, and Savitar's plain advice: farm your field.

segments.voice: Run the day backward, like a video on rewind. Dinner un-cooks. The drive home un-drives. Morning coffee pours itself back into the pot. Keep going. The house comes apart into lumber, the lumber into trees, the trees into seeds. Past the first people, the first mountains, the first stars. At some point the rewind has nothing left to rewind. What's there? Or is there even a there? One Rig Veda hymn stops at that last frame and stares at it. You glimpsed it on day one thousand fifty-seven. Today, the Nasadiya Sukta's first verse.
screen: `RUN THE DAY BACKWARD.` → `PAST THE FIRST STARS.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO REWIND.`

segments.voice: The hymn takes its name from its first words, na asat: not non-being. In paraphrase it opens: then there was not non-being, and there was not being. There was no air, and no sky beyond it. It doesn't say, in the beginning there was nothing. It says even nothing wasn't there yet. The usual pair of opposites, is and isn't, hasn't started. No air to breathe, no sky to look up into. And then, instead of an answer, the poet asks questions. What covered it? Where? In whose keeping? Was there water, deep beyond measure? That's the whole first verse: a hymn about creation that begins by refusing to describe it, and asks instead. Some readers hear wonder in that. Some hear a careful thinker, unwilling to claim more than anyone could know. Some Hindu teachers hear a picture of Brahman before names and forms. The hymn doesn't say which. It simply puts the questions into the sacred collection, to be chanted. They weren't left at the edge of scripture as doubts. They were kept inside it, and handed down with the rest.
screen: `NA ASAT: NOT NON-BEING.` · `NEITHER BEING NOR NON-BEING.` · `WHAT COVERED IT? WHERE? IN WHOSE CARE?` · `THE QUESTIONS ARE KEPT INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Let one large question come, the hymn's own if you like: what was here before anything? When an answer offers itself, set it down gently and ask again, keeping the question the way the hymn keeps its questions, open and cared for. If you pray, you can hold the question in that presence.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The Rig Veda's hymn of creation, named from its first words, not non-being, which opens with questions instead of answers.

1251.title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1251.hook: a still room, no draft, and a baby breathing. The hymn's second verse: before day and night, That One breathed without wind
1251.carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

1251.howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Nasadiya Sukta's 'That One' (tad ekam) in different ways: in Advaita Vedanta as Brahman beyond names, in devotional schools as the Lord before creation, and it is chanted as part of the Rig Veda's recited text.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's first verse: not non-being, not being, no air, no sky, and then only questions.
screen: `NOT NON-BEING, NOT BEING.`

segments.voice: A small room late at night. The window is shut. The fan is off. Not a curtain moves. In a crib in the corner a baby is asleep, and the only motion in the room is the rise and fall of that tiny chest. No wind blows anywhere. Nothing pushes that breath from outside. It comes from within, steady and quiet. A parent can stand there a long time, just listening. The Nasadiya Sukta's second verse reaches for a stillness like that, before there was a night to sleep in, and finds a breath.
screen: `A STILL ROOM. NOTHING MOVES.` → `ONE SMALL BREATH.` → `FROM WITHIN, BY ITSELF.`

segments.voice: The first verse cleared away being and non-being, air and sky. The second keeps clearing. In paraphrase: there was no death then, and no deathlessness. No sign to tell night from day. Death and its opposite, the undying: gone. Night and day, the rhythm a life runs on: gone, or not yet. And then, for the first time in the hymn, something is. That One breathed, the verse says, without wind, by its own power. Apart from it, there was nothing else at all. Not a god with a name. Not Agni, not Indra, not Varuna. Just That One, tad ekam. And not doing anything grand. It breathes. Breath is life, but here there's no air, so the breath is windless, moved by nothing outside itself. Readers take That One in different ways. Vedanta teachers in Shankara's line hear Brahman, prior to every name. Other Hindu readers hear the Lord before the work of creation. Some hear a poet pushing language as far as it goes and finding only a breath. The verse doesn't decide for them. And notice: no questions here. After the first verse's flood of them, the hymn pauses on one quiet claim. The questions will come back. For now, a breath in the stillness.
screen: `NO DEATH, NO DEATHLESSNESS.` · `NO SIGN OF NIGHT OR DAY.` · `THAT ONE BREATHED, WITHOUT WIND.` · `READ MORE THAN ONE WAY.`

segments.voice: Stop managing the breath: don't deepen it or slow it, just watch it go on its own, rising and falling with nothing outside pushing it, and rest in the stillness around it. When the mind starts to explain the breath, let the explanation go and come back to the plain fact of it; if you pray, you can rest in that breath as a gift.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation, whose second verse says: no death, no deathlessness, no night or day, only That One, breathing without wind.

1252.title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1252.hook: the power goes out on a night with no moon. the hymn's third verse begins in that kind of dark
1252.carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1252.tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1252.howItsDone: The Nasadiya Sukta is part of the Rig Veda, and like other Vedic hymns it is kept in traditional recitation, learned by memory from a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's second verse: no death, no deathlessness, no night or day, and That One, breathing without wind.
screen: `THAT ONE BREATHED WITHOUT WIND.`

segments.voice: The power goes out on a night with no moon. You shut your eyes, then open them, and can't tell the difference. The dark behind your eyelids and the dark of the room have become one dark. Your hand is somewhere in front of your face, but you couldn't prove it. Nothing has an edge. The Nasadiya Sukta's third verse begins in that kind of dark, and pushes it further than any power cut could.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `EYES OPEN, EYES SHUT: THE SAME.` → `NOTHING HAS AN EDGE.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit the verse opens tama asit tamasa gulham agre. Darkness there was, hidden by darkness, in the beginning. Not darkness covering something: darkness covering darkness. Nothing to see, and nothing to see it with. In paraphrase it goes on: all this was water, with no mark on it, nothing told apart from anything else. That's the hymn's picture of the start: not an empty space with sharp edges, but a sameness so complete that nothing could stand out. Then the turn. What was coming into being lay covered by emptiness, and that One was born by the power of tapas. Tapas is a word for heat. Later Hindu tradition also uses it for another heat, the glow a person builds through vows, fasting and long sitting. Here, at the very start, it's the warmth by which the One came to be. Notice what the verse leaves out. It doesn't say who made the heat, or name a god striking a spark. The hymn has asked questions it doesn't answer, and it keeps that honesty now. It only gives an order. First, sameness, dark on dark. Then warmth. Then one thing that could be told apart from the rest. A frozen pond is one flat gray sheet until warmth reaches it; then the ice gives, and the water starts to move. The hymn is talking about the beginning of everything, not ponds, but the shape is one a person can recognize: before anything has a name, something warms.
screen: `DARKNESS HIDDEN BY DARKNESS.` · `WATER WITH NO MARK ON IT.` · `THE ONE, BORN BY THE POWER OF HEAT.` · `SAMENESS, THEN WARMTH, THEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes or lower your gaze, and let the dark behind your eyelids be as plain as it is, without making pictures in it. Then find one warm place in the body, the breath at the nostrils, the hands resting together, the middle of the chest, and rest there, coming back whenever a thought pulls you off; if you pray, you can let that warmth be an offering.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its third verse, darkness hidden by darkness, until the One was born by the power of heat.

1253.title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1253.hook: which comes first in a morning, a thought or a want? the hymn's fourth verse gives its answer
1253.carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1253.tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
1253.howItsDone: Hindu teachers and commentators read the Nasadiya Sukta's lines on desire and the searching poets in several ways, and its verses are kept in traditional Vedic recitation learned from a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-FIFTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's third verse: darkness hidden by darkness, until the One was born by the power of heat.
screen: `DARKNESS, THEN HEAT, THEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Which comes first in a morning, a thought or a want? Watch the first minute after an alarm. Before a plan forms, there's often a lean. Toward the warm blanket. Toward coffee. Toward the phone on the nightstand. Only after the lean does the mind start talking, building reasons, making a list. The Nasadiya Sukta asks that question on the largest scale there is. The One has just been born out of the dark. What happens next? The fourth verse answers, and its answer is not a thought.
screen: `A THOUGHT OR A WANT?` → `FIRST, A LEAN.` → `THEN THE MIND STARTS TALKING.`

segments.voice: The verse opens with kama. Desire came upon it in the beginning, it says, desire that was the first seed of mind. Kama is the ordinary Sanskrit word for desire, wanting, love. It's also the name of one of the aims of a human life in Hindu teaching: pleasure and love. And here it stands at the very start, before mind. Not desire as a problem to be fixed: desire as a seed. First the wanting, then the mind that grows out of it. Then the verse turns from the cosmos to people. The poets, the kavis, searched in their hearts with wisdom, and found the bond of what is in what is not. The word for bond is bandhu. It also means kin, the people you're tied to. So the poets found that being has a kinship with non-being, a family tie running back into the dark. Notice where they looked. Not up at the sky, not into a record of what happened: in the heart. The hymn doesn't claim they saw the beginning. It says they searched inward and found a connection there. You can't go back and watch the start, but on this account you can look into your own heart and find what ties you to it. The week began with what the Rig Veda is, then settled into this hymn: neither being nor non-being, darkness on darkness, heat, and now desire, and poets looking inward for the bond.
screen: `KAMA: DESIRE, THE FIRST SEED OF MIND.` · `THE POETS SEARCHED IN THEIR HEARTS.` · `BANDHU: A BOND, A KINSHIP.` · `WHAT IS, TIED TO WHAT IS NOT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath run on its own and wait for the next thought; when it comes, don't follow it, but look just underneath for the want that came first: to be comfortable, to be finished, to be loved. Don't judge it or feed it, just notice it the way the poets searched their hearts, and come back to the breath; if you pray, you can offer each want as you find it.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. In its fourth verse, desire is the first seed of mind, and the poets find the bond of what is in what is not.
